title: The First Recorded Illusionist
description: Dionysius of Alexandria, a Greek engineer and inventor, created the first 'automatic theater' — a temple that opened its doors via steam power. This mechanical trick convinced worshippers that the gods themselves were opening the temple.

title: Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin Is Born
description: Often called 'the father of modern magic,' Robert-Houdin invented mechanical illusions that seemed impossible. He created the 'Flying Oyster' and 'The Robbing Genie' — automaton tricks that stunned 19th-century audiences.

title: The First Card Trick in Film
description: Georges Méliès, a magician turned filmmaker, used trick photography to create the first magic tricks on screen. His film 'Le Manoir du Diable' (1896) featured a bat turning into a demon — essentially a magic trick captured on film.

title: Houdini's Grand Escape
description: Harry Houdini perfected the art of escape artistry. His most famous feat: the Chinese Water Torture Cell, where he was suspended upside down in a locked water-filled glass coffin. He held the record for 21 years.

title: The Man Who Stopped Bullet
description: Joseph Dunninger, a radio magician, demonstrated his 'bullet catch' illusion live on air. He caught a real bullet between his teeth — the trick was that the bullet was actually a cork painted silver, fired from a trick gun.

title: David Copperfield's Great Wall
description: At age 28, Copperfield made the Great Wall of China 'disappear' for a live TV audience of 50 million. Using fog screens, camera angles, and audience misdirection, he created one of the most iconic illusions in television history.

title: Penn & Teller's Digital Revolution
description: Penn Jillette and Teller began revealing their secrets on PBS, changing magic forever. By showing how tricks work, they proved that knowing the method doesn't diminish the wonder — it adds a new layer of appreciation.

title: Magic Goes Viral
description: Close-up magic exploded on TikTok and Instagram. Magicians like Zach King and various street magicians reached millions, proving that magic's golden age may be just beginning in the digital era.
